The Empire State Building is an amazing sight to see.
It stands at 1,250 feet, the tallest in New York.
At the top of the building is a mast, originally planned to be used as a mooring mast for dirigibles, also known as blimps.
The architects of the Empire State Building faced many problems with putting the mooring mast on the top of the building.
They could not simply drop a mooring mast on top of the building’s flat roof.

The builders were forced to, "design a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself".
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate the new mooring mast.
Two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped, but they were unsuccessful due to forceful winds.

TAYLORSVILLE, N.C. (AP) — Where do you hide a 1,000-pound chicken?
That's what sheriff's deputies in Alexander County, North Carolina, are trying to figure out as they search for the concrete statue that disappeared from a farm west of Taylorsville over the weekend.
While the chicken may be heavy, it's only 3 feet tall.
Deputies think the statue was taken sometime between 8 p.m. Saturday and 9 a.m. Sunday from the driveway of the farm.
Chief Deputy Tod Jones told the Hickory Daily Record (http://bit.ly/2l7Z6BF) the statue's base was found several miles away.
The missing concrete bird has left the farm owners and local community puzzled and concerned.
The unique half-ton statue had become a beloved landmark in the area, attracting visitors and becoming a symbol of the farm's identity.
Authorities are urging anyone with information about the missing chicken to come forward and help solve the mystery of its disappearance.
Meanwhile, the farm owners are hopeful for the safe return of their prized concrete bird.

Many people argue that censorship is a violation of the First Amendment, which guarantees freedom of speech and the press.
However, this argument fails to recognize that there is a difference between censorship and responsible selection.
Libraries are not required to provide access to every book or other media that is produced.
Libraries have a responsibility to their patrons to provide materials that are appropriate for the intended audience.
For example, a children's library should not have books with adult content, or a library in a religious community should not have books that go against their beliefs.
It is important to remember that libraries serve a diverse community, and what may be acceptable or appropriate for one person may not be for another.
Therefore, libraries should have a selection policy that takes into account the needs and values of their community.
Additionally, some argue that censorship is necessary to protect children from harmful material.
Children are not yet mature enough to understand certain concepts and may be negatively influenced by inappropriate content.
For example, books with explicit sexual content or graphic violence may be traumatizing to a child.
Parents should have the right to restrict their children's access to certain materials, but they cannot always be present to monitor their child's reading choices.
Therefore, it is up to the library to provide materials that are appropriate for the age group they serve.
Furthermore, there are some books that are considered classics but contain offensive material.
While it is important to acknowledge the historical context of these works, it is also necessary to consider the impact they may have on readers.
For example, "To Kill a Mockingbird" is a classic novel that deals with issues of racism and prejudice.
However, it contains racial slurs that may be offensive to some readers.
In this case, it is up to the library to provide context and guidance for readers who may be affected by the offensive material.
In conclusion, while censorship may seem like a violation of freedom of speech, it is necessary for libraries to provide materials that are appropriate for their intended audience.
Libraries have a responsibility to their patrons to provide materials that are not harmful or offensive.
However, it is important to acknowledge the historical context of certain works and provide guidance for readers who may be affected by offensive material.
As Katherine Paterson said, if we start removing books that we find offensive, we may end up with no books left on the shelf for any of us.
Therefore, it is important to find a balance between censorship and responsible selection.

Alex was doing great until he sprained his ankle.
He was in a lot of pain and couldn't move his foot.
At first, Alex was really upset and frustrated.
He wanted to keep playing but he knew he couldn't.
Instead of getting angry, he took a deep breath and asked for our help.
We all rushed to his side and helped him up.
We walked him over to a nearby bench where he could rest and elevate his ankle.
While we were taking care of him, Alex remained calm and patient.
He didn't complain or get angry, even though he was in a lot of pain.
He just sat there and waited for his ankle to feel better.
We all tried to cheer him up by telling him jokes and stories, but he just smiled and nodded.
After a while, Alex's ankle started to feel better.
He slowly stood up and tested it out.
He was able to walk, but he knew he couldn't play basketball anymore.
Instead, he suggested that we go get some ice cream.
We all agreed and walked to the nearby ice cream shop.
Even though Alex was in pain and couldn't play basketball, he remained patient and understanding.
He didn't let his injury ruin our day and he even came up with a fun alternative activity.
I learned from Alex that being patient can make a difficult situation better for everyone involved.

It is the ability to endure difficult situations without complaining or getting angry.

Censorship in libraries is a controversial issue that has been debated for years.
First of all, censorship in libraries violates our freedom of speech.
The First Amendment of the United States Constitution guarantees us the right to freedom of speech.
This means that we have the right to express ourselves freely without fear of censorship or persecution.
When books, music, movies, or any other materials are censored, our rights are being violated.
We should have the right to read or watch whatever we want, as long as it does not harm anyone else.
Secondly, censorship in libraries is unfair.
One person's opinion of what is offensive may be different from another person's opinion.
Should we censor all books with violence or sex in them?
Should we censor all music with explicit lyrics?
Should we censor all movies with nudity?
If we start down this path, we may end up with nothing left on the shelves.
Finally, censorship in libraries is unnecessary.
Parents should be responsible for monitoring what their children read or watch.
It is not the job of the library to censor materials.
Libraries already have systems in place to help parents monitor what their children check out.
For example, some libraries have parental controls that allow parents to block certain materials from their children's accounts.
Parents can also talk to their children about what they are reading or watching and explain why certain materials may not be appropriate for them.
It violates our freedom of speech, it is unfair, and it is unnecessary.
Instead of censoring materials, we should focus on educating parents about how to monitor what their children read or watch.
We should also trust people to make their own decisions about what they want to read or watch.

Saeng then promises herself that she will retake her driver's test in the spring, once the hibiscus plant has budded.

She is determined to retake her driver's test and succeed.
The hibiscus plant has given her the strength to keep going and not give up.

The plant helps her to remember her past and gives her the motivation to keep moving forward.
